The British Sector of the Western Front, 1914–1918

Injuries, Treatment and the Trenches in the British Sector

Describe Two Features of [Site Focus]

How Useful Are Sources A and B?

Course Specification • Key Enquiry Sequence (1914–1918) Learnt Revised
Key Topic 5.1: The Theatre of War: The British Sector, Trench Geography & Battles
Why were trenches designed in zig-zag traverses, and how did terrain at Ypres, Somme, and Arras affect medical treatment?
Key Topic 5.2: The Trench Environment: Mud, Vermin & Non-Combat Illnesses
How did frontline conditions cause trench foot, trench fever, and dysentery, and what preventive routines were enforced?
Key Topic 5.3: Battlefield Trauma: High Explosive Shrapnel, Gas Attacks & Infection
Why did explosive artillery produce gas gangrene, and how did the Brodie steel helmet and respirators reduce fatalities?
Key Topic 5.4: The Chain of Evacuation: Stretcher Bearers, RAP, Dressing Stations & CCS
How did the RAMC and FANY evacuate wounded soldiers through six stations, and why was triage critical at CCSs?
Key Topic 5.5: Surgical Breakthroughs: The Thomas Splint, Wound Debridement & Mobile X-Rays
How did the Thomas Splint slash femur mortality from 80% to 20%, and why was Carrel-Dakin irrigation necessary?
Key Topic 5.6: Lifesaving Innovations: Blood Storage, Brain Surgery & Plastic Reconstruction
How did Oswald Robertson establish the first blood bank at Cambrai, and how did Gillies rebuild shattered faces at Sidcup?

KEY TOPIC 5.1 • ENVIRONMENTAL INQUIRY NOTEBOOK EDEXCEL GCSE (9–1) HISTORY • PAPER 1 SECTION A

How did the physical terrain and trench architecture of the British sector dictate medical evacuation and care?

Audio • Quiz
1 1914–1915• Why was the low-lying topography of Ypres a tactical and medical nightmare?
2 1914–1918• How did zig-zag traverses limit shrapnel injuries and contain shell explosions?
3 1915–1918• Why did narrow communication trenches create acute bottlenecks for stretchers?
4 Nov 1916–1917• How did the chalk geology at Arras allow safe, sterile surgical conditions?
5 1916–1917• Why did Somme and Cambrai casualties force medical evacuation reforms?
4/28 Welcome to Flanders: 500 square miles of fermented pig manure, liquid mud, and artillery with terrifying accuracy.
KEY TOPIC 5.1 • SECTION A EXAM PRACTICE EDEXCEL GCSE (9–1) HISTORY • PAPER 1 SECTION A

Question 2(a): Source Utility Assessment [8 marks • 10 mins]

SOURCE A • Contemporary Aerial Reconnaissance • Flanders Sector ORIGIN: 3 January 1918
Belgian Military Aviation vertical aerial reconnaissance photograph of the Flanders front ("Tranchée du Cimetière", 3 January 1918, altitude 1,500m), revealing zig-zagging communication trenches, traverses, and water-filled artillery shell craters across the Ypres sector.
Historical Provenance: Belgian State Archives / Aviation Militaire Belge Aerial Reconnaissance Plate Z 2842 (3 January 1918).
Study Source A. How useful is Source A for an enquiry into the defensive layout and tactical design of trench systems on the Western Front? Explain your answer, using Source A and your knowledge of the historical context. [8 marks]
Provenance Clue: Consider the nature of an official military aerial reconnaissance photograph taken over the Flanders sector in January 1918. What does an overhead view reveal about traverses, communication trenches, and shell craters, and what ground-level medical and mud conditions does it omit?
Analytical Connectives: Source A is useful for an enquiry into this topic because... • Specifically, the source reveals... • In terms of provenance, considering the author and date... • However, the utility is limited because... • Therefore...

KEY TOPIC 5.2 • ENVIRONMENTAL INQUIRY NOTEBOOK EDEXCEL GCSE (9–1) HISTORY • PAPER 1 SECTION A

Why were environmental pathogens and vermin as dangerous to British troops as enemy artillery?

Audio • Quiz
1 1914–1915• How did prolonged cold water immersion destroy tissue and produce gangrene?
2 1915–1918• Why did mandatory officer inspections succeed where voluntary advice had failed?
3 1914–1918• How did body lice cause trench fever, and how did steam baths fight it?
4 1914–1918• How did strict sanitation and chemical water chlorination prevent epidemics?
5 1914–1918• How did army responses to shell shock shift toward Craiglockhart care?
8/28 Whale oil smells like dead fish and regrets, but it beats having your toes amputated by an RAMC surgeon with a bone-saw.
KEY TOPIC 5.2 • SECTION A EXAM PRACTICE EDEXCEL GCSE (9–1) HISTORY • PAPER 1 SECTION A

Question 2(b): Follow-Up Enquiry Table [4 marks • 5 mins]

SOURCE A • Contemporary Photographic Evidence • Somme Sector ORIGIN: July 1916
Soldiers of the 1st Battalion, Cheshire Regiment occupying a captured German trench at Ovillers-la-Boisselle during the Battle of the Somme (July 1916). A sentry stands watch while exhausted infantrymen sleep huddled in waterproof groundsheets on the damp trench floor.
Historical Provenance: Official British War Photographer Second Lieutenant Ernest Brooks • Imperial War Museum (IWM Q 3990), July 1916.
Study Source A. How could you follow up Source A to find out more about the living conditions and non-combat illnesses experienced by British soldiers in frontline trenches on the Western Front? [4 marks]

KEY TOPIC 5.3 • ENVIRONMENTAL INQUIRY NOTEBOOK EDEXCEL GCSE (9–1) HISTORY • PAPER 1 SECTION A

How did high-explosive artillery trauma and chemical poison gas transform surgical treatment?

Audio • Quiz
1 1914–1918• Why did jagged shrapnel fragments cause far worse infections than rifle bullets?
2 1914–1918• Why was Clostridium welchii so lethal in deep, airless shrapnel wounds?
3 Late 1915• How did introducing the steel Brodie helmet in 1915 cut fatal head wounds?
4 Apr 1915–1916• How did the rapid evolution of chemical respirators counter suffocating gases?
5 1916–1918• Why was mustard gas far harder to counter than chlorine or phosgene?
12/28 The Brodie helmet: Looks like an upside-down soup bowl, but prevents your skull from becoming one.
KEY TOPIC 5.3 • SECTION A EXAM PRACTICE EDEXCEL GCSE (9–1) HISTORY • PAPER 1 SECTION A

Question 2(a): Source Utility Assessment [8 marks • 10 mins]

SOURCE B • Contemporary Photographic Evidence • Machine Gun Corps ORIGIN: July 1916
British Vickers machine-gun crew wearing Phenate-Hexamine (PH) anti-gas helmets with glass eyepieces and exhalation valves near Ovillers during the Battle of the Somme (July 1916).
Historical Provenance: Official British War Photographer Ernest Brooks • Imperial War Museum Photographic Archive (IWM Q 3995), July 1916.

Provenance Clue: Consider the nature of an authentic British War Office Phenate-Hexamine (PH) anti-gas helmet manufactured in 1915–1916. What physical protective properties does chemically impregnated flannel possess, and what severe combat limitations did it have in battle?

KEY TOPIC 5.5 • ENVIRONMENTAL INQUIRY NOTEBOOK EDEXCEL GCSE (9–1) HISTORY • PAPER 1 SECTION A

Why were the Thomas Splint, debridement, and mobile X-rays decisive surgical breakthroughs?

Audio • Quiz
1 1914–1918• Why was surgical excision of dead tissue more effective than chemical antiseptics?
2 1915–1918• How did continuous chemical irrigation solve the problem of deep wound infection?
3 Dec 1915–1916• How did rigid traction prevent fatal haemorrhage and shock from broken femurs?
4 1914–1918• Why was locating shrapnel on an X-ray vital before operating on gas gangrene?
5 1914–1918• Why did undetected cloth fragments remain the primary cause of post-op gangrene?
20/28 The Thomas Splint: Before Robert Jones introduced it, an 80% chance of death; after Jones, an 80% chance of living to complain about the food.
KEY TOPIC 5.5 • SECTION A EXAM PRACTICE EDEXCEL GCSE (9–1) HISTORY • PAPER 1 SECTION A

Question 2(a): Source Utility Assessment [8 marks • 10 mins]

SOURCE A • Contemporary Surgical Manual Diagram • RAMC Training ORIGIN: c.1916
Contemporary surgical training diagram illustrating the application of the Thomas Splint to a compound femur fracture: a padded iron groin ring anchors the hip while an orderly pulls the traction bandage taut along steel side-bars to keep the broken bone ends apart.
Historical Provenance: RAMC Military Surgical Instruction Manual Illustration (after Sir Robert Jones, c.1916).
Study Source A. How useful is Source A for an enquiry into the methods used to treat wounded soldiers with fractured limbs on the Western Front? Explain your answer, using Source A and your knowledge of the historical context. [8 marks]
Provenance Clue: Consider the nature of an authentic instructional diagram from an RAMC military surgical manual c.1916. What does it demonstrate about mechanical traction and splinting, and why might an idealised training diagram differ from emergency frontline conditions in a muddy aid post?
Analytical Connectives: Source A is useful for an enquiry into this topic because... • Specifically, the source demonstrates that... • In terms of provenance, considering the contemporary context... • However, the utility is limited because... • Therefore...

How did Western Front casualties drive lifesaving breakthroughs in blood storage and specialist surgery?

Audio • Quiz
1 1914–1915• How did sodium citrate liberate blood transfusion from donor-to-patient tubing?
2 1916–1917• Why was glucose addition essential to prevent red blood cell breakdown?
3 Nov 1917• Why did pre-stored blood transform surgical survival during surprise assaults?
4 1917–1918• Why did Cushing use local anaesthetic and magnets in 1917 brain surgery?
5 1917–1918• How did the tubed pedicle technique prevent skin grafts from rotting and dying?
24/28 Robertson's Blood Depot: Ice chests, sodium citrate, and refrigerated blood at Cambrai—proof that cold beer isn't the only thing worth chilling.

Question 2(b): Follow-Up Enquiry Table [4 marks • 5 mins]

SOURCE A • Primary Medical Artifact • Blood Transfusion Kit ORIGIN: 1917
Portable wooden blood transfusion and storage case used on the Western Front (1917), fitted with a graduated glass collection bottle, rubber stopper and delivery tubing, cannulae/needles, and printed War Office "Directions for Use" for citrated blood.
Historical Provenance: British Army Medical Services Transfusion Kit • Science Museum / Wellcome Collection, London (c.1917).
